title: Iran Just Fired Missiles at Three Ships in the Strait of Hormuz. India Lifted Its Emergency Gas Curbs Two Days Ago.
excerpt: The IRGC attacked a Qatari LNG tanker and a Saudi oil tanker during Khamenei's funeral procession, threatening the ceasefire that let India's energy supply chain breathe again. Oil jumped 2.5 per cent within hours.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Iran's missile attacks threaten India's energy supply chain and regional stability.
  • India lifted emergency gas curbs just two days before the missile strikes.
  • 88% of India's crude oil and 65% of LNG supply come from West Asia.
  • Oil prices surged 2.5% following the attacks, impacting India's import costs.
  • Over nine million Indians in the Gulf face economic uncertainty due to escalating tensions.

On Saturday, India's Ministry of Petroleum issued a quiet notification withdrawing the last of three emergency orders that had rationed natural gas across the country since March. The ceasefire in West Asia was holding. LNG ships were transiting the Strait of Hormuz again. The crisis, officials signalled, was over. Two days later, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps fired missiles at three commercial vessels near the mouth of the strait, setting one of them on fire. This sudden escalation raises immediate concerns for India, which heavily relies on the Strait of Hormuz for its energy imports, and for the vast Indian diaspora in the Gulf region. ## What Happened In the early hours of Tuesday, the Qatari LNG tanker Al Rekayyat was struck by a projectile — believed to be a missile or drone — on its port side while exiting the Strait of Hormuz, roughly eight nautical miles east of Limah, Oman. The crew reported an engine room fire and full smoke conditions before being evacuated. "Mayday mayday mayday. This is vessel Al Rekayyat," the captain radioed. "We are being hit by drone on port side, top of engine room. Engine room fire and full of smoke. Unable to assess further damage." A Saudi-flagged crude oil tanker, believed to be the supertanker Wedyan, was also damaged off Oman's coast. A third vessel was struck as well, according to a senior U.S. official who described the attacks as a "gross violation" of the memorandum of understanding reached between Washington and Tehran last month. Qatar's Foreign Ministry blamed Iran directly, calling the attack "a grave and explicit violation of international law" and and stating that it held Tehran "fully legally responsible for this attack and any resulting damage or repercussions." Iran has not claimed responsibility. ## Why This Matters for India India imports approximately 88 per cent of its crude oil and nearly half of its natural gas. Roughly 65 per cent of the country's LNG supply originates from West Asia, with the bulk of Qatari cargoes transiting the very waterway where Tuesday's attacks occurred. When the strait effectively closed in late February after the U.S. and Israel launched strikes on Iran, India's energy supply chain buckled. LPG imports from West Asia — accounting for nearly 60 per cent of domestic consumption — dropped to zero almost overnight. The government invoked emergency powers under the Essential Commodities Act, rationing gas supplies, diverting refinery output to LPG production, and imposing purchase limits on cooking gas cylinders. The recovery had been painstaking. Petroleum Minister Hardeep Singh Puri recently outlined how India navigated the blockade: reconfiguring refineries that had never produced cooking gas, executing ship-to-ship transfers from alternate ports like Yanbu and Fujairah, and securing new supply agreements with Algeria, Japan, and Canada. "Today, stocks are full, pumps are open, and the Indian consumer has paid less for energy through this crisis than any other consumer in the world," he wrote. Saturday's withdrawal of emergency curbs was the final signal that normal operations had resumed. Tuesday's attacks called that assessment into question before the ink was dry. The Indian Ministry of External Affairs has yet to issue a formal statement on the attacks, but officials are reportedly monitoring the situation closely, given the direct implications for India's energy security and economic stability. Any sustained disruption could lead to higher fuel prices for Indian consumers and increased inflationary pressures. ## The Ceasefire Is Fraying The attacks came during the weeklong funeral procession for Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Iran's former Supreme Leader who was killed in an Israeli airstrike at the start of the war. Hundreds of thousands of mourners thronged the holy city of Qom on Tuesday, carrying banners that read "KILL TRUMP" and chanting vows of revenge. The Revolutionary Guard, which has operated increasingly independently of Iran's civilian government, had warned ships over maritime radio in the days before the attack. "Our missiles and drones are ready to fire at you," they told vessels via VHF radio, according to a recording obtained by the Wall Street Journal. The strikes expose a deepening rift within Iran's leadership. While chief negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said on Friday that the strait should remain open because it benefits Iran's own shipping, hard-line clerics on the same day called for sinking any ship that passes "without permission." Under a memorandum of understanding reached last month, Washington and Tehran agreed to a 60-day period of negotiations toward a permanent deal. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi responded to the escalation by warning that negotiations "will not commence if threats continue." Trump, arriving at the NATO summit in Ankara, countered: "We're either going to make a deal or we're going to finish the job."

## Market Impact Oil markets reacted immediately. Brent crude rose $1.86, or 2.58 per cent, to $73.85 a barrel. West Texas Intermediate gained $1.73 to $70.28. European natural gas prices climbed as much as 4.5 per cent in early Asian trading. These price hikes will inevitably translate to higher import bills for India, potentially impacting the country's trade deficit and foreign exchange reserves. The attack on the Al Rekayyat — owned by Nakilat, the shipping arm of Qatar's LNG industry — is particularly significant because Qatar has served as a mediator in talks between Washington and Tehran. It is the first time a Qatari LNG vessel has been struck since the war began. Another Qatar-origin LNG tanker, the Al Areesh, which had been heading toward Pakistan's Port Qasim, appeared to reverse course on Tuesday after the attacks, according to shipping data. "It's clear that the risk remains," said Andy Lipow, president of Lipow Oil Associates. "Companies still have to assess whether it is worth it or not to charter oil tankers through the strait." ## What It Means for the Diaspora More than nine million Indians live and work in Gulf states — the largest expatriate population in the region. Every escalation in the Hormuz corridor directly affects their livelihoods, the economies of the countries they reside in, and the roughly $110 billion in annual remittances that flow back to India from the Middle East. The stability of the region is paramount for these NRIs, whose professional opportunities and personal safety are intertwined with geopolitical calm. India's state-owned refiner MRPL had just chartered a vessel to load crude from Iraq's Basrah terminal on July 19-20 — the first such booking by an Indian state refiner since the strait partially reopened. That shipment, and many others like it, now faces fresh uncertainty, potentially delaying crucial supplies to India. For Indian consumers, the stakes are immediate. The emergency gas rationing that ended on Saturday could return if the strait's security deteriorates further, leading to higher cooking gas prices and potential shortages. For Indian families in the Gulf, the geopolitical fault line runs through their daily commutes, their children's schools, and the ports that keep their economies moving. The prospect of renewed instability could also impact travel plans for NRIs visiting family in India or those considering returning to the Gulf for work. The 60-day negotiation window is supposed to produce a permanent peace deal. Tuesday's missiles suggest the Revolutionary Guard has a different timeline, casting a long shadow over the region and its vital connections to India.
